title: Hilda Wade
description: Published posthumously in 1900 and Allen's detective novel: a lady doctor's scientific pursuit of the man who murdered her father.
plot_or_argument: Hilda Wade, a brilliant physician and a woman of scientific genius, traces the man responsible for her father's death from a London hospital to Africa, using her medical and observational powers to anticipate his every move, in a series of episodes in which she is always a step ahead of her colleagues and the police.
historical_context: 1900: the entry of women into medicine, the imperial exploration of Africa, and the detective-fiction boom after Sherlock Holmes.
literary_significance: Hilda Wade is one of the earliest detective novels with a female scientific detective and a landmark of the woman-detective tradition: its heroine's medical expertise and her intellectual superiority to the men around her made it a forerunner of the modern female detective story.

title: Hauntings
description: Published in 1890 and the most sophisticated English collection of ghost stories: four tales in which the supernatural is a fact of place, art and psychology.
plot_or_argument: 'Amour Dure' follows a German historian in Italy who falls in love with a Renaissance murderess; 'Dionea' presents a child of Venus who destroys the men who love her; 'Oke of Okehurst' tells of a woman who becomes the double of her husband's ancestress; 'A Wicked Voice' is the confession of a composer haunted by an eighteenth-century castrato.
historical_context: 1887-90: the aesthetic movement, the Italian Renaissance revival, the new psychology of the Society for Psychical Research, and the vogue for the supernatural tale.
literary_significance: Hauntings is the finest English collection of ghost stories after Henry James and the central text of the aesthetic supernatural: its ghosts are always psychological and artistic facts, and its theory of the haunted place made it a founding text of the modern psychological ghost story.

title: Euphorion
description: Published in 1884 and Vernon Lee's masterpiece of aesthetic criticism: studies of the Renaissance in Italy and the psychology of its art.
plot_or_argument: The essays examine the Italian Renaissance through its painting, its music, its poetry and its religion: Botticelli's spring, the Florence of the Medici, the sacred music of Palestrina, the figure of the Renaissance tyrant, and the relation of art to the society that produced it.
literary_form: Studies of the Renaissance in Italy
historical_context: 1884: the Victorian enthusiasm for the Italian Renaissance, the aesthetic criticism of Pater, the new professional study of art history, and the English colony in Florence.
literary_significance: Euphorion is the central English work of aesthetic criticism of the 1880s and the finest study of the Italian Renaissance in the language: its psychological account of art and its analysis of the relation between art and society made it a landmark of English criticism and a key influence on the modern study of the Renaissance.

title: Genius Loci
description: Published in 1899 and Vernon Lee's classic of the literature of place: essays on the spirit of places in Italy and England.
plot_or_argument: The essays record the experience of particular places — Tuscan hill towns, Venetian squares, English gardens, the Roman campagna — and argue that a place has a character, a 'genius loci', which the sensitive visitor can feel and which the arts of the past have helped to create.
historical_context: 1893-99: the aesthetic travel essay, the English cult of Italy, the new psychology of place and atmosphere, and the Victorian love of the picturesque.
literary_significance: Genius Loci invented the modern essay on the spirit of place and is the finest English book of its kind: its theory of atmosphere and its prose made it a model for the twentieth-century topographical essay, and it is the source of the English literary idea of Tuscany.

title: Miss Brown
description: Published in 1884 and the most controversial English novel about the aesthetic movement: a poet's attempt to make a young woman into a work of art.
plot_or_argument: Walter Hamlin, a wealthy Pre-Raphaelite poet, takes up Anne Brown, a poor and beautiful orphan, and sets out to educate her into his aesthetic ideal; she resists, develops her own mind and conscience, and finally rejects both the poet and the society that has used her, in a novel that attacks the aesthetic movement from inside.
principal_characters: Anne Brown; Walter Hamlin; Lady Blanche; Edmund Darnley; Mrs Brown; Sacha
historical_context: 1884: the Pre-Raphaelite circle, the aesthetic movement of the 1880s, the debate on the education of women, and Vernon Lee's own quarrel with the aesthetes.
literary_significance: Miss Brown is the most important English novel about the aesthetic movement and the sharpest contemporary critique of it: its portrait of the aesthete as a self-absorbed exploiter made it a scandal in 1884, it drew an angry response from Whistler and the Pre-Raphaelites, and it is a central text of the Victorian debate on art and morality.

title: The Beautiful
description: Published in 1913 and Vernon Lee's short, lucid statement of her theory of beauty: an introduction to the psychology of aesthetic experience.
plot_or_argument: The book distinguishes the beautiful from the merely pleasant and the merely interesting, explains beauty as the satisfaction of the mind's demand for unity in variety, and treats the arts as the deliberate organisation of that satisfaction, in a compact argument that draws on her earlier physiological and psychological work.
historical_context: 1913: the new psychology of aesthetics, the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature, and the twentieth-century debate on formalism.
literary_significance: The Beautiful is the clearest English statement of the psychological theory of beauty and the summary of Vernon Lee's lifelong work in aesthetics: written for a general audience, it remains one of the best short introductions to the subject in English.

title: The History of Sir Richard Calmady
description: Published in 1901 and the boldest English novel of heredity and disability: a man born with deformed legs and his fight for the right to love.
plot_or_argument: Richard Calmady is born with his legs crushed in a hunting accident before his birth, and grows up beautiful, brilliant and mutilated; the novel follows his education, his struggle with his mother's possessive love, his travels, and his love for Honor Middleham, whom he refuses to marry because he believes his deformity makes him unfit for fatherhood, until he finally accepts his own body and his right to happiness.
principal_characters: Richard Calmady; Katherine Calmady; Honor Middleham; Julius March; Dr Knott; Lady Louisa; Roger Hensley
historical_context: 1901: the new science of heredity, the Victorian treatment of the disabled, the aesthetic cult of the beautiful body, and the English reception of Nietzsche.
literary_significance: The History of Sir Richard Calmady is a landmark of English fiction about the body and one of the boldest novels of its decade: its frank treatment of disability, sexuality and the right to love made it a scandal and a succès, and it has been recovered as one of the most important English novels about physical difference.

title: The Wages of Sin
description: Published in 1891 and Malet's most famous novel in her own time: the three generations of a family ruined by the sins of the fathers.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows the Le Mesurier family through three generations: the old Colonel's secret, his son's disastrous marriage, and the fate of the beautiful granddaughter who inherits the family curse, in a story of heredity, sexual guilt and the slow working out of a family's moral debt.
historical_context: 1891: the vogue of the heredity novel after Zola, the Victorian debate on the sins of the fathers, and the aesthetic interest in the decadent family.
literary_significance: The Wages of Sin made Malet's name and is one of the most ambitious English heredity novels of the 1890s: its three-generation structure, its religious symbolism and its frank treatment of sexual sin made it the model for the English novel of the decadent family, and it established her as one of the most daring novelists of the decade.

title: Colonel Enderby's Wife
description: Published in 1885 and Malet's first major novel: the disastrous marriage of a young woman to a man of her father's generation.
plot_or_argument: Catherine Enderby is married to Colonel Enderby, a man thirty years her senior; the novel follows her loneliness, her growing friendship with a young man of her own age, and the crisis that forces her to choose between duty and feeling, in a study of a marriage made without love.
historical_context: 1885: the debate on the age of consent and the marriage law, the New Woman controversy before its name, and the Victorian novel of the unhappy marriage.
literary_significance: Colonel Enderby's Wife is one of the strongest English novels of the unhappy marriage before the New Woman fiction of the 1890s: its analysis of a marriage made without love and its refusal of the conventional ending made it a landmark of the Victorian novel of marriage, and it established the themes that Malet would develop for the rest of her career.

title: The Far Horizon
description: Published in 1906 and Malet's finest late novel: an Anglican priest's crisis of faith and the woman he cannot have.
plot_or_argument: Dominic Iglesias, an Anglican priest and a man of extraordinary spiritual power, is torn between his vocation and his love for a woman who is free to marry him; the novel follows his struggle with the Church, with his own body and with the possibility of a life outside the priesthood, and ends with a renunciation that is also a kind of fulfilment.
historical_context: 1906: the crisis of faith in the Edwardian Church, the modernist controversy, the position of the celibate clergy, and the aesthetics of the Catholic revival.
literary_significance: The Far Horizon is Malet's most accomplished late novel and one of the most searching English novels about the priesthood: its treatment of a priest's sexuality and its refusal of easy answers made it a critical success, and it shows the religious problem novel of the 1890s carried into the twentieth century.

title: The Story of My Heart
description: Published in 1883 and the central text of English nature mysticism: the record of a soul's search for the meaning of its own existence among the fields and hills.
plot_or_argument: Jefferies recounts his childhood on the Wiltshire downs, his early sense of the beauty of the earth, his years of illness and poverty, and his conviction — arrived at in the open air — that the human soul is greater than the world and that the world is the visible body of a spiritual power.
historical_context: 1883: the Victorian crisis of faith, the Darwinian account of nature, the new interest in spiritual experience, and Jefferies's own tuberculosis.
literary_significance: The Story of My Heart is one of the great English spiritual autobiographies and the central text of English nature mysticism: its prose about the earth and the soul influenced Edward Thomas, Henry Williamson and the whole tradition of English nature writing, and it is the most personal and most radical of Jefferies's books.

title: The Amateur Poacher
description: Published in 1879 and the finest English book about the countryside from a boy's point of view: the poaching, bird-nesting and observation of a Wiltshire childhood.
plot_or_argument: Jefferies remembers the farmers, gamekeepers, poachers and labourers of his Wiltshire boyhood, the long days in the fields and woods, the trapping and the bird's-nesting, and the whole rural economy of a countryside in which every creature is either a food or a trespass.
historical_context: 1879: the agricultural depression, the game laws and the poaching wars, the decline of the rural labourer, and the Victorian country book.
literary_significance: The Amateur Poacher is a classic of English country writing and the best book of its kind about the rural world of the labouring poor: its combination of exact natural history, social observation and personal memory made it a model for English nature writing, and it is one of the finest accounts of a Victorian rural childhood.

title: The Life of the Fields
description: Published in 1884 and Jefferies's finest collection of nature essays: the meadows, woods, birds and weather of the English countryside through the year.
plot_or_argument: The essays move through the seasons and the kinds of country — the meadow, the wood, the hedgerow, the brook, the fields after harvest — recording the flowers, the birds, the insects and the farm work with an exactness that turns observation into a kind of prayer, and ending with the great essay on the wind and the sun.
historical_context: 1883-84: the English countryside before mechanisation, the agricultural depression, and the golden age of the English nature essay.
literary_significance: The Life of the Fields is the finest single collection of English nature essays of the century: its combination of exact observation and lyrical intensity made it the model for English nature writing, and it is the book in which Jefferies's genius is most consistently displayed.

title: After London; or, Wild England
description: Published in 1885 and the first great English post-apocalyptic novel: London abandoned, England returned to the wild, and a new feudal civilisation in the woods.
plot_or_argument: The novel opens with a description of the great city drowned in a lake of its own making and the country overgrown with forest; it then follows Felix Aquila, a young man of a future feudal England, who builds a canoe, sails down the Thames through the ruined city, and finds love and adventure among the remnants of a simpler civilisation.
historical_context: 1885: the Victorian fear of imperial decline, the romantic medievalism of Morris, the new scientific romance, and the industrial depression of the 1880s.
literary_significance: After London is the first great English post-apocalyptic novel and the founding text of the 'return to nature' dystopia: it anticipated The Time Machine, Earth Abides and the whole modern genre, and its vision of a drowned London is one of the most haunting images in Victorian fiction.

title: Bevis: The Story of a Boy
description: Published in 1882 and the finest English children's book of the outdoor world: two boys' summer of sailing, camping and adventure on a Wiltshire lake.
plot_or_argument: Bevis and his cousin Mark spend a summer on the island in the lake near their farm, sailing, fishing, camping, building a hut and fighting imaginary battles with the village boys, while the natural world around them is recorded in exact and loving detail.
historical_context: 1882: the Victorian country childhood, the vogue of the boys' adventure book after Treasure Island's precursors, and the natural history of the Wiltshire downs.
literary_significance: Bevis is the greatest English children's book about the outdoor world and the finest of Jefferies's books for young readers: its combination of exact natural history and the freedom of childhood made it a model for the English adventure story, and it is the English equivalent of Tom Sawyer in its picture of a boy's summer.

title: Green Mansions: A Romance of the Tropical Forest
description: Published in 1904 and the great English romance of the tropical forest: a traveller's love for the bird-girl Rima in the forests of Venezuela.
plot_or_argument: Abel, a young Venezuelan, flees into the forest after a political murder and finds a wild girl, Rima, who lives among the birds and speaks their language; he loves her, takes her to his own people for protection, and she is killed by the Indians who fear her, leaving Abel to wander the forest for the rest of his life.
principal_characters: Abel; Rima; Nuflo; Cla-cla; Runi; the Indians of the forest
historical_context: 1904: the South American travel literature of the nineteenth century, the Victorian romance revival, and the English fascination with the untouched tropical world.
literary_significance: Green Mansions is the central English romance of the tropical forest and one of the most influential novels of the natural world: Rima became one of the great mythic figures of English fiction, the novel was a best-seller on both sides of the Atlantic, and it made Hudson's name as a writer as well as a naturalist.

title: A Shepherd's Life
description: Published in 1910 and the finest English book about the rural labourer: the shepherds, downs and villages of South Wiltshire recorded from life.
plot_or_argument: Hudson records the life of Caleb Bawcombe, a Wiltshire shepherd, and through him the whole world of the downland: the sheep, the sheepdog, the yearly round of lambing and shearing, the old superstitions, the poverty and the slow disappearance of a way of life.
principal_characters: Caleb Bawcombe; Isaac Bawcombe; the shepherd's wife; Mr Hudson; the villagers of Doveton
literary_form: Impressions of the South Wiltshire Downs
historical_context: 1910: the last years of the English shepherd before the machine, the agricultural depression, and the Edwardian nostalgia for the rural past.
literary_significance: A Shepherd's Life is a classic of English rural writing and the finest book ever written about the English shepherd: its portrait of Caleb Bawcombe and its record of a vanishing way of life made it a model for the twentieth-century oral history of the countryside, and it is Hudson's masterpiece of English observation.

title: Far Away and Long Ago
description: Published in 1918 and the greatest English book of childhood in the natural world: Hudson's own boyhood on the Argentine pampas.
plot_or_argument: Hudson remembers his childhood on the pampas in the 1840s: the great plains and their birds, the gauchos and the cattle, the house and its people, the snakes and the storms, and the natural world that was for him the first and greatest of all companions.
historical_context: 1840s and 1918: the Argentine pampas before the railway, the English settler families of South America, and the Edwardian fashion for the rural memoir.
literary_significance: Far Away and Long Ago is one of the great English autobiographies and the finest book about a childhood in the natural world: its prose and its freshness made it a classic, it is the source of much of the English literary image of the pampas, and it is the best loved of Hudson's books.

title: The Purple Land That England Lost
description: Published in 1885 and Hudson's picaresque of the Uruguayan pampas: an Englishman's wanderings with the gauchos in the 1870s.
plot_or_argument: Richard Lamb, a young Englishman, flees to the Banda Oriental after a scandal and wanders the pampas with the gauchos, taking part in a revolution, falling in love, fighting duels and losing himself in the wild freedom of the plains, before returning to Montevideo and to the woman he had left.
principal_characters: Richard Lamb; Paquita; Margarita; Don Gregorio; Lucero; the gauchos
historical_context: 1885: the Uruguayan civil wars of the 1870s, the gaucho culture of the pampas, the English commercial presence in South America, and the Victorian adventure romance.
literary_significance: The Purple Land is the finest English novel of the South American pampas and one of the founding texts of the English literary image of the gaucho: its combination of picaresque adventure and exact observation made it a classic, and it was the book that gave Hudson his first reputation as a writer.

title: Lavengro: The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest
description: Published in 1851 and Borrow's strange masterpiece: the wanderings of a young scholar among the Roma, the boxers, the publishers and the roads of England.
plot_or_argument: Lavengro recounts the youth of George Borrow: his father's recruiting marches, his schooling, his apprenticeship to a solicitor, his wanderings on the road with the Romany, his encounters with the boxer, the man in black and the Armenian, and his struggles with the booksellers of London.
principal_characters: Lavengro (George Borrow); Jasper Petulengro; the man in black; Isopel Berners; the Armenian; Leonora
historical_context: 1810s-40s: the Napoleonic wars, the roads and fairs of England, the Roma of the nineteenth century, and the London book trade before the age of the cheap magazine.
literary_significance: Lavengro is one of the most original books of the nineteenth century — neither novel nor autobiography but a new form — and it is the central English text on Roma life and language: its conversations and characters have no equal in Victorian prose, and it made Borrow the model for the English literature of vagabondage.

title: The Bible in Spain
description: Published in 1843 and Borrow's most popular book: his years as a Bible agent in Spain from 1835 to 1840.
plot_or_argument: Borrow travels through Spain during the Carlist wars, distributing Protestant scriptures in Madrid, Seville, Cordoba, Galicia and the wilds of the country, and records the smugglers, the priests, the innkeepers, the gypsies and the bandits he meets, together with his arrest and imprisonment at Madrid.
historical_context: 1835-40: the Carlist wars, the Spanish Inquisition's legacy, the British and Foreign Bible Society, and the English romantic view of Spain.
literary_significance: The Bible in Spain was one of the most popular travel books of the century and the classic English account of Spain in the 1830s: its portrait of the country and its people, its dialogue and its adventure made it a best-seller on both sides of the Atlantic, and it remains the most vivid English book about Spain of the period.

title: Wild Wales: Its People, Language and Scenery
description: Published in 1862 and Borrow's great book on Wales: an Englishman's walking tour through a country he loves and whose language he has learned.
plot_or_argument: Borrow walks through north and south Wales in 1854, visiting the inns, the chapels, the castles and the mountains, and records the conversations of the Welsh people, the poetry and the language, the history of the Welsh princes, and his own fierce advocacy of Welsh culture against English contempt.
historical_context: 1854 and 1862: the Welsh language in the nineteenth century, the temperance and chapel culture, the antiquarian revival of Wales, and the English romanticism of the Celtic past.
literary_significance: Wild Wales is the finest English book about Wales and one of the great books of the nineteenth century on a Celtic language and people: its record of the Welsh language and culture at a moment of crisis made it a founding text of Welsh cultural history, and it is Borrow's most affectionate and most generous book.

title: The Romany Rye
description: Published in 1857 and the sequel to Lavengro: the scholar's further wanderings and his life with the Roma.
plot_or_argument: The narrative continues Borrow's wanderings after the departure of Isopel Berners: his stay at the Welsh inn, his journey to the fair at Horncastle, his life with the horse-dealers and the Roma, and his return to the road, with long digressions on language, religion and the character of the English.
historical_context: 1820s-50s: the horse fairs of England, the Roma, the Welsh border country, and the English road before the railway.
literary_significance: The Romany Rye completes Lavengro's strange and original project and is the most extended English record of Roma life in the nineteenth century: its horse-fair chapters and its conversations make it a classic of English travel writing, and it is the book in which Borrow's sympathy with the outcast is most fully displayed.

title: East Lynne
description: Published in 1861 and the most successful sensation novel of the century: a wife who elopes, loses her child, returns as a governess and dies of remorse.
plot_or_argument: Isabel Vane marries the lawyer Archibald Carlyle, is neglected by him, and is seduced away by the villainous Sir Francis Levison; she leaves her children, is disowned, loses her son in a railway accident, returns disguised as a governess to her own former home, and dies of grief and illness after seeing her daughter.
principal_characters: Isabel Vane; Archibald Carlyle; Sir Francis Levison; Barbara Hare; Cornelia Carlyle; Lord Mount Severn; Little Willie
historical_context: 1861: the serial market of the 1860s, the Victorian cult of the home, the law of divorce and the fallen woman, and the new railway age.
literary_significance: East Lynne was the most successful sensation novel of the century and one of the most performed plays in English: it fixed the pattern of the domestic sensation plot, its portrait of the erring wife and the lost child made it a permanent Victorian myth, and its sales and stage adaptations made Mrs Henry Wood one of the most popular novelists in the world.

title: The Shadow of Ashlydyat
description: Published in 1863 and Wood's best novel after East Lynne: a family curse, a bank failure and the destruction of a household.
plot_or_argument: The Godolphin family of Ashlydyat is haunted by the shadow that appears before a death; the bank fails through the dishonesty of one of the sons, the family is ruined, and the survivors must rebuild their lives, while the shadow appears again before the final catastrophe.
principal_characters: Thomas Godolphin; George Godolphin; Maria Godolphin; Janet Godolphin; Margery; Mr Snow; Lady Godolphin
historical_context: 1863: the banking failures and commercial panics of the 1850s-60s, the Victorian family firm, and the fashion for the sensation novel with a supernatural apparatus.
literary_significance: The Shadow of Ashlydyat is the finest of Wood's later novels and one of the best English sensation novels of the 1860s: its combination of family curse, commercial disaster and domestic realism made it a favourite, and it shows Wood's characteristic power of making the ordinary household the site of terror.
